Senses.Note: Three Tier 2 works transmit one Baizhang-Huangbo case with distinct later verses. J34 B299's section heading confirms an old-case-and-verse unit but does not prove the individual capping verse's named author. X83 repeats the lineage prose with an additional comparison and is not needed after the three J readings.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB441.xml). Tongzhen of Wanfeng gives a closely parallel Huangbo biography: Baizhang tells of the shout he received from Mazu, and Huangbo grasps its point. Senses.Explanation: A lineage narrator reports Huangbo understanding when Baizhang recounts Mazu's shout; three later verse settings treat that one event. Huangbo asks Baizhang about the earlier lineage. Baizhang recounts a second visit to Mazu, whose shout had left him deaf for three days, and the narrator says Huangbo understood. The J34 Sanfeng volume places the old clause in an orig-and-commentary case-and-verse sequence; its following verse interprets Mazu's and Baizhang's force, but the local heading does not individually name the verse author, so that voice remains unattributed. Qiaosongyi's J39 lineage section repeats the old clause and adds a verse on receiving the force of the shout. Tongzhen of Wanfeng repeats the same narrative and gives a different verse on Huangbo's grasp of the encounter. These are three later poetic readings of one Baizhang-Huangbo event, not three separate realizations; the headword itself is narrator prose, not Huangbo's speech.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the sixteen-foot golden body
AlternateTargets: a sixteen-foot golden buddha-body
Senses.Note: The sixteen-foot golden body is the imposing Buddha form. Chan teachers place it beside a blade of grass or even a dung heap to unsettle a fixed separation between revered form and ordinary things; a monk may also ask about it directly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 便能拈一莖草。作丈六金身。將丈六金身。却作一莖草。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄). In a hall address after a monk asks about losing both mind and Buddha, Dahui Zonggao describes realizing their nonduality in daily life. He says one can then make a single blade of grass into a sixteen-foot golden Buddha body and turn the golden body back into grass. The pair expresses freedom of use, before Dahui sharply warns his audience not to cling to the achievement.

HeadwordSpanReview.GrammarEvidence: Dahui Zonggao repeats 丈六金身 in one reversible grass/body transformation statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百草頭上無邊春信手拈來用得親丈六金身功德聚等閑擺手入紅塵
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C078/C078n1720.xml). Chan School: Comprehensive Linked-Pearls Collection of Verse Commentaries on Old Cases (禪宗頌古聯珠通集). After the old case of a future Buddha spreading hair over mud before Dīpaṃkara and a patron marking a temple site, a capping verse attributed in the source to Tiantong Jue, Hongzhi Zhengjue, says that the merit-filled sixteen-foot golden body can step casually into red dust. The Buddha image enters ordinary life in Hongzhi’s own verse; it is not spoken by the figures in the case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X64/X64n1260.xml). Outline Record of the Successive Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄). When imperial incense arrives, Mi’an Xianjie addresses the hall and praises the freedom of a monk who can use the Chan staff and board without being bound by forms. In that setting he says one can make a blade of grass into the sixteen-foot golden body and then turn the body back into grass. This is Mi’an’s own hall speech, not Yuanwu Keqin’s.

HeadwordSpanReview.GrammarEvidence: Yuanwu Keqin repeats 丈六金身 in one reversible grass/body transformation statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 糞掃堆頭現丈六金身，且拈在一邊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate’s “Raising Old Cases” (宗門拈古彙集). Commenting on a line of the Third Patriarch’s Trust in Mind inscription, Xuedou Chongxian says the golden Buddha body appearing atop a dung heap should be set aside, and even a towering presence on the flesh body deserves a blow. The contrast deliberately places the exalted form in an impure setting; Xuedou voices the later appraisal.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120) (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)). In a hall address, Yuanwu Keqin quotes Layman Pang’s verse on the selection ground for buddhas, then praises Pang as able to make a blade of grass into a sixteen-foot golden body and back again. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元). In the section for the monk of Yaoshan in Raozhou, an unnamed monk asks what the sixteen-foot golden body is. The master answers with an unexpected image of a judge deciding a case and a high official changing it. The phrase belongs to the questioner’s request for the Buddha form, while the Yaoshan master voices the reply.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names the Buddha’s majestic golden body. Dahui Zonggao says a person free of fixed mind/Buddha distinctions can turn a blade of grass into the golden body and back. Mi’an Xianjie uses the same reversible image in a separate imperial-incense hall address. Hongzhi Zhengjue’s verse lets the merit-filled golden body step into ordinary dust, while Xuedou Chongxian pointedly imagines it atop a dung heap. Yuanwu Keqin praises Layman Pang for the grass-and-body turn but says it still falls short of the highest barrier. In a different lamp encounter, an unnamed monk simply asks the Yaoshan master what the golden body is and receives an oblique reply. The figure names the Buddha’s majestic body even where it is brought into contact with lowly or everyday things.

Senses.Explanation: Miyun closes two different sermons by urging a person of resolve to act on their own strength instead of following another person's tracks. At the end of a summer retreat Miyun tells the monks that this is the time to go their own way and closes with the soaring-ambition couplet. In a later sermon requested by a lay donor honoring his parents, he uses the same couplet after speaking about the hearers recognizing their own source. These are two occasions in one Miyun record and one work family. An unnamed monk brings the line to Feiyin after asking who can smile in his crowded assembly; Feiyin calls it a forced show of boldness. A different monk brings it to Linye after an extended exchange; Linye replies that he still cannot leap out. The couplet is an exhortation in Miyun's voice and a tested boast in the monks' mouths.

Entries.SourceTerm: 丈夫自有衝天志，不向如來行處行

Senses.PreferredTarget: A person of resolve has an aspiration that reaches the sky and does not merely walk where the Tathagata walked.
AlternateTargets: A person of resolve has an aspiration that reaches the sky and does not merely walk where the Tathagata walked.
SearchAliases: a person of resolve has an aspiration that reaches the sky and does not merely walk where the tathagata walked
Senses.Note: Urge independent realization rather than imitating the Buddha path as a fixed track. The saying does not reject the Buddha; it resists copying a precedent without seeing.

Senses.Explanation: A person of resolve has an aspiration that reaches the sky and does not merely walk where the Tathagata walked. Urge independent realization rather than imitating the Buddha path as a fixed track. Tianyin Yuanxiu and Yi'an Shanzan use the complete saying in distinct recorded teaching turns. Danxia Dangui, Miaoyun Zhenxiong give further current deployments. The saying does not reject the Buddha; it resists copying a precedent without seeing.

Senses.Explanation: Changlu sets independent action against following even the Tathagata’s tracks: the true man’s own energy surges to the sky. Changlu asks where someone beyond choosing one side and escaping the other actually walks, then gives the full couplet. The line contrasts one's own sky-surging energy with following the Tathagata's path.

Senses.Explanation: Shut your dog-mouth is a blunt imperative to stop speaking. Touzi Yiqing directs it at an attendant who keeps talking, Miyun Yuanwu gives it as a short reply in a monk's questioning sequence, and Zhaozhou Congshen repeats Yaoshan's wording before adopting the same instruction himself. Baoning Renyong supplies it as replacement speech in a separate old-case comment.

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 向荊棘林中出手去也

Senses.Explanation: To mix water and mud: to enter the messy particulars of a situation and respond there. Chan masters use the image for public teaching and for taking up an inherited encounter, often while testing whether such engagement can coexist with independence. Liao'an Qingyu strings the phrase with riding a thief's horse and turning heaven and earth, then answers a monk imagined to challenge his silent debate. Yunwai Xingze says that releasing his staff means mixing water and mud and extending himself to beings, while taking it back means standing alone. Zhe'an Jingfan calls his responses to people high and low mixing water and mud while reviewing his own record of teaching. Yuan'an Liao puts the phrase after a demand for a direct, economical approach and asks whether his listeners can get beyond the Buddha's silence. Gumei Dinglie takes up an older exchange about crossing water and names his own verse-like response mixing water and mud. Yuanwu Keqin says that, if no extraordinary person answers, he must mix water and mud and reach into a thorny grove; he then raises his whisk before the assembly. Jieshi Zhipeng places the phrase in a field-side hall address and asks why someone who has obtained the whole still has only half.

Senses.Explanation: A conforming or pat phrase: an answer that fits a ready verbal pattern. The phrase has 143 exact occurrences in 96 source files representing 93 works. Its defining proverb says, ‘One conforming phrase ties up a donkey for ten thousand ages.’ Yuanwu Keqin uses the label as an immediate verdict on an answer and warns, ‘Take care against conforming phrases.’ Yunwai Ze lists stock replies—including ‘when the sky is clear the sun comes out’ and ‘when it rains the ground is wet’—as dead sayings delivered as conforming phrases; elsewhere he describes people using such phrases when questioned. Yuanwu says his own teaching seat does not make conforming phrases or look-alike phrases. Later commentary can dispute the verdict: Yushan Shangsi says that treating Yunmen Wenyan’s ‘the body exposed in the golden wind’ as a conforming phrase fails to recognize it.

Senses.Explanation: A monk gives this follow-up line in three separate exchanges, and each teacher answers differently. In Yunwai Xingze’s hall, a monk asks what it is like to let go at the cliff. Yunwai says that would be just the time to receive a blow. The monk follows with the exact line about passing it on, and Yunwai answers that the monastery gate opens toward the south. At Gumei Lie’s winter-retreat release, a questioning monk asks first about binding and then about release. After Gumei gives an instruction for the road ahead, the monk bows and says the exact line; Gumei strikes him and warns against false words. In Dahui Zonggao’s opening sermon, a monk presses him through the contrasting San Sheng and Xinghua formulas for going out and not going out. Dahui answers each turn. The monk then offers the exact line, and Dahui replies that Jingshan has lost the advantage today. In each case the monk treats the teacher’s response as something to carry forward, while the teacher refuses to let that declaration settle the exchange.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The moon curves like a bow: little rain, much wind.
AlternateTargets: A bow-shaped moon foretells scant rain and plenty of wind.
SearchAliases: bow moon little rain much wind
Senses.Note: The pair is a weather saying about a curved moon and the likelihood of wind rather than rain. Huangbo speaks it in an older assembly case, recounted across the corpus. Muyun poses it as a live test; Poshan both uses and displaces it; Jie'an, Zhulang, and Yuanjie give it as the close of their own challenges. The saying can sound like an omen, but each current turn makes the listener answer in the present encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Taiyuan Yin answers a monk who asks which patron's invitation to accept; later teachers use the image to question narrow choice and to address their own supporters. In the old encounter, an unnamed monk asks Taiyuan Yin which household he should visit when several patrons invite him. Taiyuan answers that the moon is reflected in a thousand rivers and every gate has a monk. Danxia Zichun retells the exchange and adds a verse on a single formless presence appearing in many forms. Linquan raises it as a numbered case and criticizes the monk's small calculation about invitations. In an independent hall address, Yuanjie Ying uses the same couplet while answering supporters who have repeatedly asked him to resume teaching at a monastery.

Senses.Explanation: The moon reflected in moving water becomes a question about who can receive or express what is seen. Jifei Ruyi uses the line to answer why the Buddha appears to be born although the pure body has no coming or going. Chisong Daoling recounts giving it as his reply when Jiufeng asks him to show his understanding. Yuejian asks it in a memorial hall address after evoking the water of Lake Tai. Feiyin Tongrong closes an address by raising a whisk and posing the same moon-in-water question. Each use turns the image into a live prompt rather than an account of a celestial event.

Senses.Explanation: The bright moon reveals the person walking at night is a poetic capping line built from a visible scene: moonlight makes a night traveller visible. Foyan Qingyuan closes his verse on Gold-Ox's meal call with it after saying to leap free of Gold-Ox's den (跳出金牛窠窟子). Erzhan Zun asks who the onlookers at Shakyamuni's birth declaration are (且道誰是傍觀者) and, after a pause, answers with the line. Hanxiu Ruqian uses it to close a verse addressed to Zhao Naichen after telling him to point a golden whip beyond the clouds (試把金鞭雲外指). Tui'an Xian makes the image's revealing force explicit: ‘do not say that hiding leaves no trace’ (莫謂藏身無影迹), because moonlight shows the traveller. These uses preserve one visible image while giving it different local targets; they do not establish a fixed identity for either the moon or the traveller.

Senses.Explanation: "The moon enfolds the distant cassia; stars cluster around the North Star" joins two celestial images. Masters use the complete couplet as a compact answer or ending, especially where an occasion calls for an elevated image. Yun'e uses it at an opening address; Dabian gives it in a birthday exchange. Juelang answers a Pure Land question with it; Baiyu ends a blessing for an opening with it. Minshu gives it in a direct encounter reply.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi explicitly raises Yunju You's four-line verse: the moonlight and pine-sound couplet, followed by 'What a true message; look carefully.' He compares its direct presentation to a mute serving as interpreter and says his visit to Baolin suits this season. He then responds separately to each line, with images of dwelling under green cover, the bright moon, cold that leaves no foothold, looking back, and sitting deep in the mountains listening. At the end he asks whether his commentary reaches the old master's meaning, and answers with a late-returning iron flute and an openly displayed household style. The first complete verse is Yunju's; the elaborations and final question are Wuyi's. Yunju You, the name printed in Wuyi's attribution, is another recorded name of Yunju Yuanyou. He is distinct from Huanglong.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. At a winter-solstice address, Baichi raises his whisk and asks an approaching monk whether he can join the rare melody of a single thread of spring. The monk gives the headword. Baichi says he is not yet a knowing companion; when the monk remains standing, he tells him to withdraw. A subsequent question about winter receives a plum-blossom answer, and Baichi's address later raises Zhaozhou's instruction to wash the bowl. The couplet is the unnamed monk's response, not Baichi's own approved explanation of the season. The rebuke is part of the retained exchange and prevents treating the lovely scene as sufficient recognition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. Guxue opens an address during confinement for retreat by saying the person without rank sweats despite having no form. He asks why, then gives the couplet. He next raises Linji's encounter in which the monk is seized when asking about that person, and adds Changsha's verse on the sameness of all things. Guxue says the two elders exert their full force but people still misread them; striking his staff, he contributes his own image of a tiger biting a tiger and a mud snake swallowing a venomous snake. The couplet is Guxue's present application before the old cases, not part of Linji's quoted speech or a statement that the formless person lacks bodily activity.

In the Huanglong selection, the complete four-line verse appears before images of dark clouds over Zixiao peak and white waves rising in Poyang Lake. Huanglong then speaks of uncontrived activity and warns that calculation puts one a vast distance away. Taking up his staff, he describes disruptive use against Maitreya's eyes and the patriarch's nose, and asks why Linji and Deshan laugh before shouting. This local window does not name Yunju as the earlier verse's author; that attribution rests on Wuyi's explicit named parallel. The opening inherited verse must remain separate from Huanglong's counterimages, staff gesture, and concluding question. Yunju You, the name printed in Wuyi's attribution, is another recorded name of Yunju Yuanyou. He is distinct from Huanglong.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi explicitly raises Yunju You's four-line verse: the moonlight and pine-sound couplet, followed by 'What a true message; look carefully.' He compares its direct presentation to a mute serving as interpreter and says his visit to Baolin suits this season. He then responds separately to each line, with images of dwelling under green cover, the bright moon, cold that leaves no foothold, looking back, and sitting deep in the mountains listening. At the end he asks whether his commentary reaches the old master's meaning, and answers with a late-returning iron flute and an openly displayed household style. The first complete verse is Yunju's; the elaborations and final question are Wuyi's. Yunju You, the name printed in Wuyi's attribution, is another recorded name of Yunju Yuanyou. He is distinct from Huanglong.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 下座。尼超方請上堂。僧問：「不下笠子勘俱胝，請師分明通二句。」師舉拂，云：「何似生？」進云：「秪如尼撩起便行，未審具什麼眼？」師云：「頂門亞一隻。」進云：「可謂千峰勢到嶽邊止，萬泒聲歸海上消。」師云：「闍黎分上，且喜沒交涉。」問：「大事未明，如喪考妣，和尚已明，如喪考妣作麼？」師云：「被闍黎帶累。」尼問：「是法住法位，世間相常住，如何是常住相？」師云：「師姑原是女人做。」乃云：「宏機獨唱，地覆天翻；正令當行，星飛電捲。惟許超方作者始透閞牢，倘或鼠膽之流，望崖何啻？事弗獲已，未免按下雲頭，道箇山是山、水是水，男是男、女是女，僧是僧、俗是俗，各住其位、各安其居，有般沒鼻孔底又卻向背地裏冷笑，謂百山愛說老婆禪，好與三十拄杖。是即也是，百山總未甘在。何故？驅耕奪食渾閒事，帶水拖泥看轉難。」上堂。僧出位擬問，師云：「若是久經行陣者，何須立地念篇章？」便下座。冬至，上堂。僧纔出，師舉拂，云：「一線陽春曲，繇來和者稀，闍黎還和得麼？」僧云：「月色和雲白，松聲帶露寒。」師云：「未是知音者。」僧佇立，師云：「且退。」問：「如何是冬來意？」師云：「幾點梅花帶雨開。」僧禮拜，云：「去也。」師云：「得閒折取一枝好。」乃云：「群陰消剝盡，忽地轉和陽，葭管吹灰煖，梅梢噴雨香，不是世諦流布，亦非佛法商量。君不見？疏山老，善舉揚，有人參問冬來意，向道京中出大黃。」復舉僧問趙州：「學人乍入叢林，乞師指示。」州云：「喫粥了也未？」僧云：「喫粥了也。」州云：「洗缽去。」其僧有省。師頌云：「粥罷令伊洗缽盂，天風不費巧工夫，時來自解翻身去，萬里江山啟畫圖。」上堂。「明如杲日，寬若太虛，不可以識識，不可以知知，百山山裏三十年前有箇奇怪精靈，迸出頭來直得山崩地坼，過後杳不見形蹤。」驀拈拄杖，云：「看看：如今又出頭來也，是汝諸人還有住腳處麼？」便下座，一齊打散。李弘英、弘彥慶父誕，上堂。僧問：「從心之歲古稱少，今朝海屋喜添籌，如何是因齋慶讚一句？」師云：「拄杖粼粼八尺長。」進云：「恁麼則山靈共祝無窮壽，海眾同瞻壽日明。」師云：「不似山僧說得親。」乃云：「壽似虛空亙莫量、壽如松柏迥蒼蒼、壽猶巨海不枯竭、壽比靈龜算倍長，以此稱壽，可謂至矣。然虛空、松柏猶有焦殞之期，巨海、靈龜豈無終盡之日？不如就人人本有底鋪華錦上去也。」

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. Guxue opens an address during confinement for retreat by saying the person without rank sweats despite having no form. He asks why, then gives the couplet. He next raises Linji's encounter in which the monk is seized when asking about that person, and adds Changsha's verse on the sameness of all things. Guxue says the two elders exert their full force but people still misread them; striking his staff, he contributes his own image of a tiger biting a tiger and a mud snake swallowing a venomous snake. The couplet is Guxue's present application before the old cases, not part of Linji's quoted speech or a statement that the formless person lacks bodily activity.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 泉歸宗麻谷禮拜國師南泉歸宗，麻谷禮拜國師三人同行，必有我師。擇其善者而從之，其不善者而改之。玄沙三種病人玄沙三種病人一二三，見聞覺。更是誰，頓消爍。花簇簇處鷓鴣啼，草薰薰時鴛鴦飛。玄沙老，玄沙老，賴過當年欠一著。諦當之言徒唯然，中間樹子半零落。靈雲桃花靈雲桃花子路當時問要津，滔滔天下丈夫人。相逢相見若如此，更有春風春又春。禾山打鼓禾山打鼓解打鼓，幾打鼓，四打鼓，打破鼓，天界地界莫莽鹵。分明記取好參詳，李陵曾入番人戶。寄書來報漢朝臣，黃沙漫漫無由住。黃龍南禪師語嗣慈明黃龍南禪師語嗣慈明語要上堂：僧堂覰破看積廚，鴟𩾲咬殺佛殿脊。明明向道尚乃不會，豈況盖覆將來？擊禪牀，下座。智海無性，因覺妄以成凡。覺妄元虗，即凡心而見佛。只麼休去，便道同安無折合。隨汝顛倒所欲，南斗七，北斗八。青蘿寅緣，直上寒松之頂；白雲淡泞，出沒太虗之中。萬法本閑，唯人自鬧。閙箇什麼？咄！順捋虎鬚應自顧，倒拈蝎尾任他猜，胡來漢現尋常事，勿將明鏡掛高臺。擊禪牀，下座。月色和雲白，松聲帶露寒。好箇真消息，憑君子細看。紫霄峯頂，黑雲靉靆。鄱陽湖裏，白浪滔天。一氣無作而作，萬法不然而然。更若思量擬議，迢迢十萬八千。拈拄杖，云：橫拈倒用，撥開彌勒眼睛；暗去明來，敲落祖師鼻孔。當是時也，目連鵞子飲氣吞聲，臨濟、德山呵呵大笑。且道笑箇什麼？喝一喝。千般說，萬般諭，只要教君早回去。去何處？良久，云：夜來風起滿庭香，吹落桃花三五樹。說妙談玄，乃太平之姦賊。行棒行喝，為亂世之英雄。英雄姦賊，棒喝玄妙，皆是長物，黃栢門下總用不著。且道黃栢門下尋常用箇什麼？喝一喝。人人盡握靈蛇之珠，箇箇自抱荊山之璞，不自回光返照，懷寶迷󳬛不見道。應耳時，若空谷，大小音聲無不足。應眼時，如千日，萬像不能逃影質。擬議若從聲色求，達磨西來也大屈。古人看此月，今人看此月。如何古人心，難向今人說。古人求道內求心，求得心空道自親。今人求道外求聲，尋聲逐色轉勞神。勞神復勞神，顛倒何紛紛。擊禪牀，下座。世間有五種不易：一、化者不易；二、施者不易；三、變生為熟者不易；四、端坐喫者不易。更有一種不易是什麼人？良久，云：聻。便下座。時真點胷作首座，藏主問云：適來和尚道：第五種不易是什麼人？首座云：腦後見腮，莫與往來。示眾。身口意清淨，是名佛出世。身口意不清淨，是名佛滅
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1318.xml). Continued Essentials from the Sayings of Ancient Worthies. In the Huanglong selection, the complete four-line verse appears before images of dark clouds over Zixiao peak and white waves rising in Poyang Lake. Huanglong then speaks of uncontrived activity and warns that calculation puts one a vast distance away. Taking up his staff, he describes disruptive use against Maitreya's eyes and the patriarch's nose, and asks why Linji and Deshan laugh before shouting. This local window does not name Yunju as the earlier verse's author; that attribution rests on Wuyi's explicit named parallel. The opening inherited verse must remain separate from Huanglong's counterimages, staff gesture, and concluding question. Yunju You, the name printed in Wuyi's attribution, is another recorded name of Yunju Yuanyou. He is distinct from Huanglong.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 月色和雲白，松聲帶露寒

Senses.Explanation: Moonlight shares the clouds' whiteness, while pine sounds carry the cold of dew. The sensory images are the opening of a four-line verse that calls them a true message and asks the hearer to look carefully. Wuyi explicitly attributes that verse to Yunju You, another recorded name of Yunju Yuanyou, then gives his own extended line-by-line response. In the Huanglong selection the same complete verse is not locally named; its earlier attribution therefore depends on Wuyi's named parallel, while the dark clouds, towering waves, and staff action that follow belong to Huanglong. Elsewhere a monk offers the couplet to Baichi and is told he is not yet a knowing companion; Guxue uses it in his own question about how the formless person without rank sweats. The notes preserve those different uses. A vivid description of cold or clarity is not automatically a successful answer, and the scene should not be turned into a fixed code for an unseen object.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Moonlight is seen in stillness; the sound of a spring is heard in seclusion.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敢問大眾：既是斤兩分明，為甚却不知落處？拈起拄杖，云：時人只看絲綸上，不見蘆花對蓼紅。眼若不睡，諸夢自除。心若不異，萬法一如。恁麼告報，且從諸人點頭。忽若心眼雙忘，又作麼生？春風初解凍，枯木也生花。有句無句，如藤倚樹。眼睛定動，失却巴鼻。忽然拈得時如何？水向竹邊流出冷，風從花裏過來香。向上一路，千聖不傳。學者勞形，如猿捉影。承天今日貴買賤賣去也。拈起拄杖云：月色靜中見，泉聲幽處聞。沙彌披剃，云：斷除鬚髮著僧衣，精進當遵古佛儀，一念不生親領略，方知我法妙難思。便恁麼是真出家，可以報生成之德，可以酬莫大之恩；其或未然，無人知此意，令我憶南泉。上不在天，中不在人，下不在地，還知落處麼？卓拄杖，云：一片月生海，幾家人上樓？昔有僧辭趙州，州云：有佛處不得住。師云：魚行水濁。無佛處急走過。師云：草偃風行。三千里外逢人不得錯舉。師云：泗州人見大聖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1318.xml). Continued Essentials from the Sayings of Ancient Worthies. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1405.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shixi Xinyue. Shixi Xinyue addresses his assembly after an occasion connected with the monastery and its supporters. He asks how the gathered teaching can be witnessed, pauses, and closes with the exact moonlight-and-spring-sound couplet. Shixi is the current hall speaker; the image is shared wording, not proof of his authorship of the old saying.

Senses.Explanation: An anonymous older saying about quiet perception is quoted in a preface, then used by two teachers in separate sermons. A preface to Chisong Ling's poetry quotes the couplet as an ancient saying and asks why the moon and spring, available everywhere, seem open especially to a quiet person. In a separate X68 teaching, a Chengtian teacher raises his staff and speaks the line while turning from clever verbal distinctions to seeing and hearing directly. Shixi Xinyue later closes a hall address on receiving and showing the teaching with the same moonlight-and-spring-water image. The three contexts use the wording for different immediate purposes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有問生從何處來。便道水流元在海。死向何處去。遽謂月落不離天。似此等見解。喚作喫鐵棒陷鐵圍之張本。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B25/B25n0145.xml). Extensive Record of Zhongfeng Mingben of Tianmu (天目中峰廣錄). Zhongfeng Mingben warns an assembly against borrowed phrases used to dismiss the matter of birth and death. He imagines someone answering “Where did birth come from?” with water always flowing in the sea, then answering “Where does death go?” with the moon setting without leaving the sky. Zhongfeng rejects this ready-made understanding as grounds for severe error unless the speaker has actually awakened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「潮去還歸海。」進云：「如是則涅槃城裏翻身轉，直踏毘盧頂上行。」師云：「月落不離天。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin (費隱禪師語錄). At a memorial hall address requested by Lady Tao and her sons for her deceased husband Changyuan, a monk asks Feiyin Tongrong for a word on birthlessness. Feiyin first replies that the departing tide returns to the sea. When the monk elaborates with an image of turning within nirvana, Feiyin answers that the moon sets without leaving the sky. Senses.Explanation: The moon sets without leaving the sky: apparent departure does not take it outside its encompassing field. Jingyin Daozhen uses the line in a court memorial exchange after Empress Cisheng’s death; Feiyin Tongrong answers a later memorial question with the same moon-and-sea pairing. Gusu Zun brings the image to a new-year question about what lies beyond new and old. Songlai Quan sets it beside “mind is Buddha” in a short address and tests the assembly with his whisk. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies a sharp limit: he quotes the line as the sort of stock answer to a death question that is dangerous without actual awakening. These are separate uses rather than repeated records of one event.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Yushan asks a monk what happens after moonset, then challenges the monk’s reply.

Senses.Explanation: The moonset question presses a lay visitor, a monk, and two funeral or interview settings. Miyun asks a lay visitor what happens after the moon sets when the visitor offers the image of one moon reflected in a thousand rivers; the visitor cannot answer, and Miyun strikes. In a separate hall, the Dongshan teacher asks a monk the same question after the monk says that the moon appears beneath the water and the bright sun shines above. The monk hesitates and is struck. Luyan He uses the question in his own cremation address for a laywoman, immediately answering with an image of flames rising on an icy river and lotus flowers in fire. At Yushan, a teacher asks a monk where the master of dreamless awareness is; when the monk says the moon shines in an empty sky, the teacher asks the exact moonset question. The monk gives a further answer, and the teacher presses him again. Across these sources, a bright image is tested by what happens when its light changes or disappears.

Entries.SourceTerm: 月落潭無影，雲生山有衣

Senses.PreferredTarget: The moon sets, and the pool has no reflection; clouds rise, and the mountain is clothed.
Senses.Note: The same natural changes answer a teaching question, close a memorial question, and cap a compiled account of Guishan and Yangshan. A fixed moon/substance and cloud/function code is not stated by the retained passages.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。僧問：「拈花契旨，故是嘉聲克肖；面壁投誠，灼然悟非尋常。育聖淘凡人共委，洞水逆流請舉揚。」師云：「燭曉玉人初破夢，夜寒青女未登機。」進云：「夜半正明，天曉不露。如何是正位一色？」師云：「青山常舉足，白日不移輪。」進云：「銀碗盛雪，明月藏鷺。如何是大功一色？」師云：「碧海銀魚躍，蘆花白鳥栖。」進云：「續鳧截鶴，夷嶽盈壑。如何是今時一色？」師云：「月落潭無影，雲生山有衣。」進云：「恁麼則曹溪意旨唯師得，洞上綱宗獨我聞。」師云：「假雞聲叫難顢我，未肯糢糊放過關。」便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB363.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wenmunian. Wenmu Nian answers a monk's successive questions about the 'one color' of the proper position, great achievement, and the present time. His first answers give green mountains moving and the sun not moving, then silver fish in the blue sea and white birds among reeds. The moon disappearing from the pool and clouds clothing the mountain answer the third question. When the monk declares that the master alone has Caoxi's purport and that he alone has heard the Dongshan lineage, Wenmu says an imitated cockcrow cannot fool him, refuses a vague passage through the gate, and strikes. The pair is one precise reply within the sequence, not a certificate for the monk's ensuing claim of exclusive understanding. The headword is rendered: The moon sets, and the pool has no reflection; clouds rise, and the mountain is clothed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 對靈，小參。問：「四大分張向什麼處去？」師云：「天然無相子，不挂出塵衣。」僧云：「兩手撥開生死路，翻身直入白雲鄉。」師云：「一物不生全體現，目前光彩阿誰知？」乃云：「佛性場中，纖毫不動，心隨境轉，境隨心生，離色離相，塵盡光生，忘形忘跡，體露真空，到這裏，有什麼生死去來、遷流之變？豈不聞釋迦老子云：『諸行無常，是生滅法，生滅滅已，寂滅為樂。』汝等諸人還識得這寂滅為樂的消息麼？若識得寂滅為樂的消息，無來無去，無生無死，無是無非，無彼無此，乃至四聖六凡及一切有情無情無不寂滅。既然如是，只如今日所薦亡靈高門舒氏向什麼處去聻？」良久，云：「月落潭無影，雲生山有衣。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB474.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liaozong of Panshan. Liaozong Chaojian speaks at a memorial assembly for a deceased woman of the Shu family. The opening question asks where the four elements go when they separate. His address speaks of forms and traces being forgotten, quotes the Buddha on cessation as happiness, and asks whether the assembly knows that purport. He then returns the question to the person being commemorated: where has she gone? After a pause he gives the moon-and-cloud pair. The images describe disappearance of a reflection and a newly clothed mountain without naming a place to which the deceased has traveled. They form the answer to the memorial's question, rather than a map of an afterlife. The headword is rendered: The moon sets, and the pool has no reflection; clouds rise, and the mountain is clothed.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2006.xml). Eyes of Humans and Devas. The third occurrence is the compiled expositional voice in Eyes of Humans and Devas, not a new utterance by Guishan or Yangshan. It introduces their style through responsive acts, then raises the tea-picking exchange: Guishan hears Yangshan but does not see him; Yangshan shakes a tea tree; they challenge each other's command of substance and function. The exposition sums this up as using an occasion and obtaining substance without contrivance, then asks whether the reader wants to see Guishan and Yangshan. The moon-and-cloud pair is its own closing presentation. Its absence and appearance sit after that account of responsive handling; neither image is explicitly assigned a permanent separate definition. The headword is rendered: The moon sets, and the pool has no reflection; clouds rise, and the mountain is clothed.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Feiyin Tongrong asks his attendant Lingji what Xinghua intended by striking Kebin. Lingji answers that one who loves a child does not see the child's ugliness. Feiyin presses him: if the blow was compassion, why was Kebin driven out? Senses.Explanation: Sumeru is the named cosmic mountain used as a vast landmark, comparison, carried burden, or direct answer. Chan records keep the mountain visible while making it stand in exchanges beside mustard seeds, oceans, nostrils, and the act of walking around it. The full "Mount Sumeru" (須彌山) occurs 1,052 times and the variant transliteration "Sumeru-lu" (須彌盧) 147. Chan records use the mountain's name in questions, comparisons, and statements of size or destruction. One Compendium saying places together "break Sumeru into fine dust" and "take the waters of the four great seas into one hair-pore" (破須彌為微塵。攝四大海水入一毛孔。). A Continued Lamp address says, "if the lineage purport is raised, Sumeru must directly be shattered" (舉揚宗旨。須彌直須粉碎。). A Dahui lamp recension says, "pick up Sumeru-lu in the palm and swing inside a needle's eye" (拈須彌盧於掌上，向針眼裡打鞦韆). Gulin Qingmao also supplies a local self-definition: "the so-called Mount Sumeru is precisely the move before living beings and buddhas were established" (所謂須彌山者，即是生佛未具已前一著子也). Public exchanges and addresses place a seamless stupa and an unstruck bell on Sumeru's summit, tie Sumeru with a lotus-root filament, and test the claim that a mustard seed contains it. These are the records' stated uses; Gulin's equation does not replace the proper name throughout the corpus.

Senses.Explanation: Mount Sumeru is the inherited world-mountain and, in one famous exchange, Yunmen's entire answer. When asked whether there is fault in not producing a single thought, Yunmen says only “Mount Sumeru”; Wansong then records several rejected explanations of that reply. Elsewhere the mountain retains its ordinary cosmological identity while serving comparisons: Wuzu Fayan says his stance is like leaning against it, Gulin Qingmao writes of lifting it away, and a cited scripture imagines chewing or carrying it. Those figurative actions depend on the mountain's proverbial enormity, but they are not repetitions of Yunmen's case.
Senses.Note: The name denotes the inherited world-mountain. Yunmen also gives that name alone as an answer; later authors quote, compare with, lift, chew, or carry the mountain without turning all uses into that case-answer.

Senses.Explanation: To strike a golden bell on the summit of Mount Sumeru is a stock line used in public addresses, exchanges, and later case-raising. Yuanwu Keqin gives it after contrasting Xuefeng and Xuansha; Liao'an Qingyu places it beside hearing the water-clock at the Five Phoenix Tower; an unnamed monk repeats that paired line to Yuanwu; and Wuzu Shijie gives it as the second answer in the raised Zhimen exchange. The records preserve the action and location without defining the bell beyond the line itself.

Senses.Explanation: Jiufeng sets a condition when the assembly asks the head monk to succeed Shishuang. After Shishuang dies, the assembly asks its head monk to take the teaching seat. Jiufeng Daoqian, who served Shishuang, says the successor must first understand the former teacher’s intent. The head monk asks what that intent is, and Jiufeng presses him with Shishuang’s sayings about resting, cold ashes, an old incense burner, and white silk. A J teacher cites the succession dispute, an X record gives Jiufeng’s exchange, and another X work discusses it.

In Sanshan Denglai's small assembly, the person who scales the unapproachable mountain turns a somersault at its summit, and the one who enters the unfathomable sea emerges through the clouds. Sanshan closes with the selected formula. When a monk steps out, he asks for the sentence not transmitted by a thousand sages; the monk nods, and Sanshan descends. The capable person is presented through this demanding imagery and subsequent test, rather than identified as an independent historical traveler.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB485.xml). Pumen Dengxian writes in reply to Sanyi of Nanbin, greeting spring renewal and the golden-haired lion's roar at Nanbin Wanshou. He gives the formula and congratulations, then regrets that obligations prevent his joining the colleague's teaching seat. He continues by asking where his brother can now open his mouth after the activity has already shown itself everywhere. Here the clause recognizes a colleague's capacity within a particular letter, with Sanyi as source-named recipient rather than its speaker.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB244.xml). In Sanshan Denglai's small assembly, the person who scales the unapproachable mountain turns a somersault at its summit, and the one who enters the unfathomable sea emerges through the clouds. Sanshan closes with the selected formula. When a monk steps out, he asks for the sentence not transmitted by a thousand sages; the monk nods, and Sanshan descends. The capable person is presented through this demanding imagery and subsequent test, rather than identified as an independent historical traveler.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 鄉，四顧徬徨，一帶寒煙荒坰，總屬眾生業感，居士以為何如？倘念疇昔知交，至情骨肉，那玉治平一晤，不獨蓬薜生輝，便是再生良晤。復楚省童真和尚書復楚省童真和尚書八經寒暑，兩辱佳音。昨接雲章，三番又至。柰弟年來癖懶成性，未及回音，幾拂來意。若非手足相關，不幾以不情視之耶？殊不知正是我弟兄親切處。只這親切處，國一馬師猶落下風，思備雪峰猶剩白紙。這裡說甚福盈福虧，苦樂安養？四無量何據何憑？鈍阿羅是真是假？遊戲神通非分外，美食不中飽人餐。既能快活優游，誰是寂寥境界？湖北之山，兄無住足。花冠萎墜，弟等何干？若云會聚之緣，不須彈指，蓋其中自有不隔者在也。臨穎神馳，依依不盡。復南濱三一和尚復南濱三一和尚雷驚出蟄，雨化從新，桃花浪暖時，南濱萬壽金毛哮吼，須是恁麼人，始解恁麼事。賀賀！茲以薄務縈身，不及握椎座右，共唱卷阿，實深抱歉。雖然，一昌眾甫，化母機梭蚤已逗漏于山前嶺後，更看阿兄復從何處啟口？復靜默上座復靜默上座來札殷勤，深感關切，正謂水乳蘭蒞，馨味自投，知我者其誰歟？今不能無說，但當此時世，隱處為高，其奈欲隱彌露？所以古人居山林、隱朝市，或出或處、或語或默，總皆方便機權。若論箇裡關頭，最難透過。果爾透得過，客歲玉乾處境不曾逢、今日夔門亦不曾別，說甚舊歲新春、悲懽離合、鶴跡翩翻之語，個中消息已露；獅音海底之言，無耳偏能得聞。猿腸寸斷我知音，爐鞴欲開君自得，不須捨此覓彼，直須密在汝邊，不妨反覆二三，莫作口頭讀過。復睿珍單傳二座復睿珍單傳二座年來虧二座導引，勷厥勝事，總欲智行兩全，方是聖賢能事。唯願二座日

Senses.Explanation: The formula ties understanding to the person capable of meeting the matter, but such a person is shown differently in each setting. It can close a teacher's challenge, question whether an old participant was a knowing companion, or praise a colleague by letter. When a monk offers the formula as his answer, Tongzhen asks whether he really understands it that way and drives him out with blows. In Sanshan Denglai's small assembly, the person who scales the unapproachable mountain turns a somersault at its summit, and the one who enters the unfathomable sea emerges through the clouds. Sanshan closes with the selected formula. When a monk steps out, he asks for the sentence not transmitted by a thousand sages; the monk nods, and Sanshan descends. The capable person is presented through this demanding imagery and subsequent test, rather than identified as an independent historical traveler. In a separate case comment, Sanshan quotes Touzi pointing to a stone and saying all Buddhas are inside, Xuefeng saying someone is not inside, and Touzi returning to his hut. Sanshan says the matter should be brought out before a fellow traveler and concealed without a knowing companion. He asks whether Xuefeng is such a companion and gives the formula, followed by a new misty mountain-path verse. This is Sanshan's present appraisal of the old interaction, not a line spoken by Touzi or Xuefeng. Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji gives a compact hall talk listing self-binding without rope, gouging sound flesh, drawing a prison on the ground and fabricating a lie from empty space. He then ends with the formula. The person capable of understanding must meet these apparently self-created complications; the text does not name a privileged individual or explain them as four doctrinal categories. The line belongs to Tiebi's current conclusion. Wanfeng Tongzhen raises an old Juyun interview in which the teacher demands an immediate answer and strikes the hesitant monk out. He asks a current monk what old Juyun intended. The monk answers with the selected formula; Tongzhen asks whether he takes it that way and also strikes him out. Senses.Note: Wangshan Ti says that one must know the honored person apart from the honored position; only then can honor escape a ladder of ranks. Huigong admires the subtlety yet asks whether Wangshan is beyond criticism. Zhe'an answers the old saying with an image of an empty palace and a rooster at dawn. Suru would strike Wangshan for still placing the person on a ladder, while Wansong asks what happens when the paired positions cross. The line is a test of how a living person uses a position without becoming it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998B.xml). Dahui Pujue’s Armory of the Chan School. Zhang Shangying, called Wujin, wrote the pair after consulting Doushuai Congyue about Huitang Zuxin. The inherited fist test made naming the fist a touching and refusing the name a turning away; Zhang's verse claimed another subtle accord beyond these alternatives. Its rhinoceros image suggests intimate connection, rather than identifying a separate physical organ of realization. Dahui Zonggao says that people once admired the verse, but that trying to see Huitang through it would leave one far away. He regrets that Zhang had died before he could confront him. He then raises Lingyuan's praise of Huitang and Huang Luzhi's ridicule of putting an ear-hole into empty space. Zhang remains the exact quoted verse speaker; Dahui's present critical raising denies that the clever contrast can simply certify Zhang's understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉無盡居士詢晦堂家風於兜率恱欲往就見恱云此老只一拳頭耳師喝一喝恱廼潛奉書於晦堂云無盡居士世智辯聰非老和尚一拳垂示安能使其知有宗門向上事耶師又喝一喝無盡訪晦堂堂果示以拳頭話無盡默計不出恱所料由是易之有偈云久向黃龍山裏龍到來只見住山翁須知背觸拳頭外別有靈犀一點通師云著賊了也二大老何以隨人󱯾跟轉兜率悅是何心行耶蒼天蒼天。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (L/L154/L154n1639.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianyin Xiu. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the visit in stages. Doushuai tells Zhang that Huitang has only a fist; Tianyin interjects a shout. Doushuai secretly writes to Huitang that only a display of the fist can make this clever official recognize the matter beyond; Tianyin shouts again. When the meeting unfolds as predicted, Zhang takes Huitang lightly and voices the four-line poem ending in the headword. Tianyin says they have met a thief and asks why the two elders turn along at someone else's heels and what sort of conduct Doushuai is displaying, crying out to heaven twice. Thus Zhang's pair is quoted within a current criticism of how the whole encounter was arranged. The source does not offer a new hidden point beyond the fist as Tianyin's own approved solution.

Occurrences.Kwic: 黃司李入山請陞座僧問當初無盡居士見兜率悅禪師既有契證因詢晦堂家風於悅欲徃就見悅曰此老只一拳頭耳意旨如何師云明破即不堪僧云悅乃潛奉書於晦堂曰無盡居士世智辯聰非老和尚一拳垂示則安能使其知有宗門向上事耶如何是宗門向上事師便打僧云未幾無盡遊黃龍訪晦堂於西園先以偈書默菴壁曰亂雲堆裏數峰高絕學高人此遯逃無奈俗官知住處前驅一喝散猿夔徐𧥣宗門事晦堂果舉拳示之意旨又如何師舉拄杖云貫得其便僧云無盡默計不出悅之所料由是易之無盡既有契證何得隨人脚跟轉師云汝那裏見無盡恁麼說來僧無語師云卻是汝隨別人語生解僧云無盡有偈曰久嚮黃龍山裏龍到來只見住山翁須知背觸拳頭外別有靈犀一點通又作麼生師云無盡只顧出身處不知話作兩橛僧云恁麼則無盡不唯不知晦堂用處且不識兜率話頭也師云放汝兩頓棒乃云昨晚無舌說今朝呈醜䂐耳聞兼目見不間僧與俗選佛與選官同體不同服不以服飾觀便見真面目箇箇本成現人人皆具足常說熾然說不消三寸舌所以道迦葉不聞聞世尊不說說不墮悄然機動容揚古路下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (L/L154/L154n1640.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun Wu. At an address requested by an official, a monk asks Miyun Yuanwu through the old visit step by step. Miyun replies that exposing the device spoils it, strikes at the question about the matter beyond, and raises his staff when asked about Huitang's fist. When the monk says Zhang had followed another's heels, Miyun asks how he knows that, then says the speech is the monk's own derivative understanding. The monk quotes Zhang's couplet and asks how it is. Miyun says Zhang only attended to a way of getting out and did not know that his speech had split in two; he does not specify a single fixed division here. The monk adds a stronger judgment against Zhang, and Miyun spares him two rounds of blows. His closing verse includes monks and laypeople and says that differing robes should not determine how one sees the true appearance. The exact pair is still Zhang's quoted voice, now used to test a present questioner as well as the old literary claim.

The exact pair is still Zhang's quoted voice, now used to test a present questioner as well as the old literary claim.

Entries.SourceTerm: 須知遠煙浪，別有好商量

Senses.PreferredTarget: Know the far mist and waves: there is another way to discuss the matter
AlternateTargets: Beyond those distant waves lies another fitting conversation
SearchAliases: beyond distant waves another way to discuss
Senses.Note: The first clause points toward far-off mist and waves; the second says there is still another fitting way to discuss the matter. Tian'an and Zixian use the pair in direct replies. Yushan turns it into an answer for the New Year; Muyun, Guantao, Miaoyun, and Gumei use it after inherited cases, and Baiyu brings it to a question about place. The imagined distance keeps the present speaker from treating the preceding answer as the last word. Reader prose explains the headword-bearing unit within each retained window; neighboring independent addresses in oversized KWIC windows are not treated as part of the same encounter.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Tian'an Sheng answers a monk during an address. The monk has asked whether the dragon girl's immediate becoming Buddha came from her own understanding or a teacher's transmission; Tian'an accepts neither alternative. The monk then asks why Sudhana, if he could finish the matter in a single undertaking, still traveled through more than a hundred and ten cities. Tian'an answers with the mist-and-waves pair. The line withholds the tidy conclusion that an immediate result makes further travel pointless. The next question begins a separate exchange about meeting face to face; it is not an explanation supplied by Tian'an for this answer.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Yushan Shangsi gives an imagined New Year exchange in his own tea talk. He first says that the ancients' assertions and denials about New Year's Buddha teaching both fall into faulty talk. Asked what the teaching is, he would say, 'Go on as before.' Asked why he says this when it is a new year, he would answer with the mist-and-waves pair. The headword therefore answers the objection to his first reply; Yushan does not specify an alternative doctrine behind it. Both question and answer are staged in his present speech, not reported as a historical visitor's words.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB184.xml). Seven-Session Recorded Sayings of Monk Muyun. Muyun Tongmen raises a monk asking Shushan about winter's arrival; Shushan answers that the capital produces rhubarb. Muyun then offers his own answer to the same question: lotus shells from Xinghua are good for making a fire. He warns that treating this as worldly circulation has not even dreamed of Buddha teaching, but discussing it as Buddha teaching is thousands of miles away. Asked how it ultimately is, he closes with the headword. The pair follows his rejection of both kinds of explanation. Xinghua here belongs to Muyun's proposed winter answer, not the name of the older question's respondent.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB287.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zixianjue. At Zixian Jue's installation at Longyuan, a monk asks about the assembly before him rather than his changed title as abbot. Zixian replies, 'One prize, two contests.' The monk then says that everywhere green willows can tether a horse and every house has a road through to Chang'an. Zixian meets that expansive claim with the headword. The monk shouts; Zixian says, 'A good shout.' After the monk bows, he adds that the cat has bitten through the hemp. His later address reuses the monk's roads-and-willows line, so the exchange is not a simple prohibition of those words: the headword intervenes in how they are being offered at this moment.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu. Baiyu Jingsi speaks as a mountain monk visiting Pingzheng Court. He says city and mountain are not separated; even hesitating about separation puts another speck into the eye. Raising his whisk, he tells the assembly that seeing through here allows entering the marketplace to help people: the crossroads do not leave the solitary peak, nor the peak the crossroads. He then asks how to speak when both ends are cut off and no middle is established, and gives the headword. Its position after that question prevents 'city and mountain are the same' from becoming the whole answer. No audience reply is recorded before the next address begins.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB362.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guantaoqi. Guantao Daqi quotes Fu Dashi's verse about sleeping and rising with Buddha, inseparable like shape and shadow, ending that this very speaking voice is where to find Buddha. Guantao calls this speaking in two separate pieces and says that under the patch-robed monk's gate it cannot even save itself. He asks why, then supplies the headword as his own conclusion. The mist-and-waves line belongs to Guantao's criticism, not Fu's verse. The record calls the verse speaking in two pieces without specifying precisely which division Guantao means; it does not spell out another positive definition in the closing pair.

Miaoyun Zhenxiong raises Pang Yun asking Zechuan, while tea is being picked, whether Zechuan sees him when the dharma realm cannot contain his body. Zechuan replies, 'Had it not been this old monk, I would nearly have answered you.' Miaoyun appraises both men and says both must receive blows. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB463.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gumeilie of Weishan. Gumei Dinglie raises Ehu's questioning of learned monks about the Way in walking, standing, sitting and lying down. Ehu rejects knowledge, nondiscrimination, and the four Chan composures and eight attainments as sufficient answers; the group falls silent. Dahui Zonggao later comments with a taunting pair about letting the other person answer back in a quarrel or pour water when spat at. Gumei says that old Miaoxi, Dahui, has applied the wrong wording, then gives the headword. This is Gumei's reservation about Dahui's comment, not a fourth answer originally offered to Ehu. The monk has asked whether the dragon girl's immediate becoming Buddha came from her own understanding or a teacher's transmission; Tian'an accepts neither alternative. The monk then asks why Sudhana, if he could finish the matter in a single undertaking, still traveled through more than a hundred and ten cities. Tian'an answers with the mist-and-waves pair. The line withholds the tidy conclusion that an immediate result makes further travel pointless. The next question begins a separate exchange about meeting face to face; it is not an explanation supplied by Tian'an for this answer.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Yushan Shangsi gives an imagined New Year exchange in his own tea talk. He first says that the ancients' assertions and denials about New Year's Buddha teaching both fall into faulty talk. Asked what the teaching is, he would say, 'Go on as before.' Asked why he says this when it is a new year, he would answer with the mist-and-waves pair. The headword therefore answers the objection to his first reply; Yushan does not specify an alternative doctrine behind it. Both question and answer are staged in his present speech, not reported as a historical visitor's words.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB184.xml). Seven-Session Recorded Sayings of Monk Muyun. Muyun Tongmen raises a monk asking Shushan about winter's arrival; Shushan answers that the capital produces rhubarb. Muyun then offers his own answer to the same question: lotus shells from Xinghua are good for making a fire. He warns that treating this as worldly circulation has not even dreamed of Buddha teaching, but discussing it as Buddha teaching is thousands of miles away. Asked how it ultimately is, he closes with the headword. The pair follows his rejection of both kinds of explanation. Xinghua here belongs to Muyun's proposed winter answer, not the name of the older question's respondent.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB287.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zixianjue. At Zixian Jue's installation at Longyuan, a monk asks about the assembly before him rather than his changed title as abbot. Zixian replies, 'One prize, two contests.' The monk then says that everywhere green willows can tether a horse and every house has a road through to Chang'an. Zixian meets that expansive claim with the headword. The monk shouts; Zixian says, 'A good shout.' After the monk bows, he adds that the cat has bitten through the hemp. His later address reuses the monk's roads-and-willows line, so the exchange is not a simple prohibition of those words: the headword intervenes in how they are being offered at this moment.

Senses.Explanation:
Know the far mist and waves: there is another way to discuss the matter.

Tian'an Sheng answers a monk during an address. The monk has asked whether the dragon girl's immediate becoming Buddha came from her own understanding or a teacher's transmission; Tian'an accepts neither alternative. The monk then asks why Sudhana, if he could finish the matter in a single undertaking, still traveled through more than a hundred and ten cities. Tian'an answers with the mist-and-waves pair. The line withholds the tidy conclusion that an immediate result makes further travel pointless. The next question begins a separate exchange about meeting face to face; it is not an explanation supplied by Tian'an for this answer.

Yushan Shangsi gives an imagined New Year exchange in his own tea talk. He first says that the ancients' assertions and denials about New Year's Buddha teaching both fall into faulty talk. Asked what the teaching is, he would say, 'Go on as before.' Asked why he says this when it is a new year, he would answer with the mist-and-waves pair. The headword therefore answers the objection to his first reply; Yushan does not specify an alternative doctrine behind it. Both question and answer are staged in his present speech, not reported as a historical visitor's words.

Muyun Tongmen raises a monk asking Shushan about winter's arrival; Shushan answers that the capital produces rhubarb. Muyun then offers his own answer to the same question: lotus shells from Xinghua are good for making a fire. He warns that treating this as worldly circulation has not even dreamed of Buddha teaching, but discussing it as Buddha teaching is thousands of miles away. Asked how it ultimately is, he closes with the headword. The pair follows his rejection of both kinds of explanation. Xinghua here belongs to Muyun's proposed winter answer, not the name of the older question's respondent.

SearchAliases: a dew-cold pine beyond the peaks
Senses.Note: The J29 line is Dabian’s answer after the assembly falls silent; in J39 Luyan speaks it after slapping a disciple. The subsequent old cases do not supply its speaker.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB463.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gumeilie of Weishan. Gumei Dinglie asks his hall where one stands after stepping beyond a high pole, strikes his staff, and voices the dew-cold pine line before raising another old case.

Senses.Explanation: Three teachers speak the mountain-pine line in a hall challenge, a disciple test, and an exhortation on a lofty vantage. Dabian Xianquan asks his assembly to show the higher opening after he has commented on an older teacher’s verse. Nobody answers; he takes down his whisk and gives the pine line himself. In Luyan He’s recorded tests, a disciple replies to the question about a phrase that cuts through birth and death; Luyan slaps him, voices the same line, and keeps testing what the disciple has grasped. Gumei Dinglie presses a hall about stepping beyond the top of a pole and turning from a cliff, strikes his staff, and closes with the line before introducing a separate Dami-Mazu case. The exact 峰 spelling and three different settings are preserved.

Senses.Explanation: Subhuti is a named disciple whom Chan masters repeatedly place inside questions about speaking, hearing, sitting, and what counts as seeing the Buddha. Yongming Yanshou quotes Subhuti asking whether equality is conditioned or unconditioned. Dahui Zonggao and Zeng Kai raise the rock-sitting case in which flowers fall and Subhuti denies having spoken a word. Yuanwu Keqin tests the exchange with the flower-scattering god, while Shakyamuni Buddha invokes Subhuti’s rock seat in rebuking the nun Utpalavarna. These are the uses stated in the records; the entry does not reduce him to a generic imported emblem of emptiness.

Entries.SourceTerm: 鴈影落寒潭，孤舟橫野渡

Senses.PreferredTarget: A wild goose shadow falls on the cold pool; a lone boat lies across the country ferry.
Senses.Note: The two passages use the same scene as a reply, once in an address and once at the scattering of bones. They supply no fixed separate meanings for goose shadow, cold pool, boat or ferry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。云：萬壑千巖，雲霞鎖霧，洞然明白，覿面分付。還有知時別宜底麼？良久，云：鴈影落寒潭，孤舟橫野渡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1378.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuming Huixing. Wuming Huixing gives the pair in his own address. He starts with a thousand ravines and cliffs under clouds and mist, yet calls it all plainly clear and directly handed over. He asks whether anyone knows the time and what is fitting, pauses, and answers with a goose shadow falling into a cold pool and a lone boat lying across a rural ferry. The next landscape is therefore his answer to the question about recognizing the occasion, not a separate report of a journey. The text names neither a particular pool nor a destination for the boat, and does not decode one image as one fixed doctrine. The headword is rendered: A wild goose shadow falls on the cold pool; a lone boat lies across the country ferry.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The title names Wuming Huixing, whose hall address contains this final answer. No canonical roster name matches this identity; Wuming Huijing is a different master and must not be substituted. Complete address, title, TEI header and collected parallel checked.

Entries.SourceTerm: 鴈無遺蹤之意，水無留影之心

Senses.PreferredTarget: The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain its reflection.
SearchAliases: goose leaves no intended trace water retains no intended reflection
Senses.Note: The pair describes a response without deliberate retention; it does not say that no reflection appears or prescribe inertness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 秉拂。「心同虛空界，示等虛空法，證得虛空時，無是無非法。且虛空作麼生證？秋風清，秋月明，秋聲瑟瑟，秋色盈盈，秋蟬歷歷，秋鳥嚶嚶，秋陽杲杲，秋漏沉沉，秋鐘遲入夢，秋水炤空清，秋華香陌隴，秋露溼雲陰。現前一眾光輝溢目，寂爾無垠，盡凡聖情、脫知見縛，赤體擔荷得去，如龍得水、似虎靠山，倚天長劍逼人寒，神威凜凜。杲日當空，無不炤光彩澄澄，便見移法界于豪端，擿大千于方外，小兒伎倆；攪長河為酥酪，變大地作黃金，野老家私；無邊剎境，自它不隔於豪端，話作兩橛；十世古今，始終不離於當念，添足畫蛇。所以道：靈光不昧，萬古徽猷，入此門來，莫存知解。直下如鴈過長空、影沉寒水，鴈無遺蹤之意、水無留影之心。到者裏，釋迦讚嘆不及、達磨有口難宣；二祖承虛，道箇覓不可得；龐公接響，自誇及第心空；百丈峰頭，野鴨子點胸點肋；鼇山店裏，鱉鼻蛇擺尾搖頭；黃檗一條拄杖化作獰龍，龍潭半橛紙條炤出猛虎。從上若佛、若祖、若善知識、若老和尚，無不從此一印印開，一證永證。故經云：『若人欲識佛境界，當淨其意如虛空，遠離妄想及諸趣，令心所向皆無礙。』非虛語也。祇如竿木隨身，逢場作戲，又作麼生？逢著上大人，便說可知禮。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. In an autumn whisk instruction, Tian'an Sheng asks how one realizes space itself. After enumerating autumn wind, moon, birds and light, he says the assembly is filled with brightness and must cast off attachment to views and explanations. The goose crossing the sky and its reflection in cold water then become his present comparison: neither leaving a trace nor retaining an image requires an intention. He follows with earlier teachers' responses and asks how one performs freely wherever one meets the occasion. The pair describes an uncontrived response amid what appears, not the disappearance of appearances or permission to stop examining one's conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪眾打七畢，秉拂。「般若如大火聚，近之則燎卻面門。誠哉是言，到者裏卜箇五雙，無你湊泊咀嚼處、無你思量卜度處。有般依艸附木底漢，見說青青翠竹無非法身、鬱鬱黃花無非般若，一據據定，更不移易絲毫。殊不知，一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛。所以道：『言前薦得，猶迷顧鑑之端；句下明機，亦是觸途狂見。』假饒不承言、不滯句，脫略窠臼，別轉機關。」卓拄杖，云：「中心樹子猶未屬你在，放開也在我、捏聚也在我。放開一線也，紫羅帳裏撒珍珠，剝名品荔枝安汝口內，只要滋味親知；捏聚將來時，活逼生蛇頭戴角，要令石女當下生兒，只教卓地無錐。雖然，費醬傷鹽，笑破老胡脣吻，其如鴈過長空、影沉寒水，鴈無遺蹤之意、水無留影之心，說甚麼麻三觔、乾矢橛、鋸解稱鎚、即心非心，大如兄、小如弟，庭前柏樹、青州布衫、金剛圈、栗棘蓬。」驀喝一喝，云：「者些祭鬼神茶飯不消秉拂一喝，百雜碎了也。且超然獨脫一句又作麼生？舉手攀南斗，回身倚北辰，出頭天外看，誰是我般人？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. After the community's seven-day session, Yikui Yuankui criticizes people who seize a sentence about bamboo or flowers and never move from it: even an apt phrase can become a stake tying a donkey for ages. He alternates releasing and gathering through vivid images, then compares the movement to a goose and its reflection, neither intending to leave nor retain a trace. A shout shatters the familiar case-phrases he has just listed, and he asks for a sentence of independent release. The headword is Yikui's own present comparison. Its lack of intention is set against clinging to sayings, not offered as another fixed saying to cling to.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (L/L154/L154n1639.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianyin Xiu. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises Tianyi Yihuai's address: a goose crosses the sky and casts its reflection in cold water without either goose or water intending to preserve a trace. Tianyi connects this with moving among different kinds without forcing them into sameness, and contrasts free use with not using it at all. Tianyin's added verse asks who dares such movement, gives a tiger growing horns, and returns to the high goose and shadow on the autumn river before a blind turtle laughs. The exact pair remains Tianyi's quoted voice; Tianyin's new verse actively handles it rather than merely copying it. The final fantastic images are not decoded into a stable hierarchy of people or mental states.
